claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 1, run a realistic cumulative-edit benchmark comparing parameter-based editors against the unedited model and a parameter-free baseline. Use public COUNTERFACT and ZSRE edit sets with GPT-J and GPT-2-XL or another openly available HuggingFace backbone, and apply ROME, MEMIT/MEND where available, constrained fine-tuning, and an in-context or retrieval-based method such as IKE/SERAC-style inference-time editing. Filter to examples the base model can answer, then perform sequential no-rollback edits at batch sizes 1, 10, 100, and 1000. After each edit block, measure Reliability on edited prompts, Generalization/Paraphrase Score on equivalent prompts, Locality/Neighborhood Score on out-of-scope prompts, and unrelated capability damage on HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and Natural Questions perplexity or accuracy. If parameter editors preserve high Reliability and Generalization while maintaining locality and unrelated-task performance as edits accumulate, the claim that they cannot reliably update knowledge without damage is weakened. If edit success remains high only for isolated rollback edits but locality, perplexity, or downstream task accuracy degrades cumulatively, the claim is supported. This experiment could be made less necessary by existing public sequential-edit logs across the same models, editors, edit counts, and unrelated capability tasks rather than only single-edit aggregate scores.

With respect to evidence piece COUNTERFACT evaluation suite, replicate the near-perfect editing results under increasingly realistic evaluation variants. On COUNTERFACT and ZSRE, reproduce the original ES/PS/NS aggregate scores for ROME, MEMIT, and MEND under their standard single-edit rollback protocol, then re-score the same edits using stricter paraphrase sets, semantically checked neighborhood prompts, portability probes such as subject-replace/reversed/one-hop questions, MQuAKE-style multi-hop questions if available, and held-out unrelated prompts. Include pre-edit, fine-tuning, and in-context baselines, and report not only aggregate Score S but the full Reliability, Generalization, Locality, Fluency, Consistency, and mean-rank/perplexity changes. If near-perfect scores persist across paraphrases, portability, multi-hop propagation, and unrelated capabilities, the subclaim that prior results fail realistic evaluation is weakened. If scores collapse outside canonical prompts or are accompanied by locality and fluency degradation, it supports the claim that prior results are evaluation-fragile. This experiment could be made unnecessary by audited benchmark releases that already include validated paraphrases, nontrivial portability probes, human-checked prompts, and non-rollback evaluation for the same prior methods.

To address subclaim 4, directly test the proposed geometric mechanism by measuring whether localized weight edits are amplified along low-variance representation directions and whether that predicts global propagation and compounded damage. For each edited fact in COUNTERFACT or ZSRE, collect hidden states from a large public text sample such as WikiText-103 or C4 validation prompts, estimate each edited layer’s representation covariance spectrum, decompose the pre/post-edit activation change induced by ROME/MEMIT/MEND into principal-component directions, and compute amplification as change magnitude divided by the baseline variance along each direction. Then evaluate whether low-variance-direction amplification predicts changes on unrelated prompts, locality failures, perplexity increases, and degradation after 10/100/1000 sequential edits, controlling for layer, edit norm, relation type, and baseline fact confidence. Replicate with representation zeroing or causal tracing to separate geometry from a tracing artifact. If damage and global propagation are strongly predicted by low-variance amplification even after controls, the geometric limitation hypothesis is supported. If edit damage is explained mainly by edit size, layer choice, implementation, or dataset relation, and low-variance directions add little explanatory power, the geometric subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released activation-difference/covariance analyses showing the same low-variance amplification pattern across models, editors, and datasets.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direction-resolved, variance-normalized measurement of activation change that tests whether amplification is concentrated in low-variance directions and increases with cumulative edits across methods and model settings.
